flags.message: outcome.json records interim_signals.amicus_briefs = 0, but the 2026-09-04 snapshot shows an amicus brief (Initiative and Referendum Institute) submitted Sep 03 2026, the same day as the denial. The docket lists the denial entry before the amicus entry, so a count cut at the order plausibly gives 0; worth a look because the interim-v1 amicus-increment claim resolves on this field for all three candidates. Not corrected here - the outcome is not mine to edit.

codex-baseline's retrieval.md describes three CourtListener MCP opinion searches and a fetch of the 43-page application PDF; its retrieval_log.json (coverage 0.6, 10 rows) carries none of those calls, only statpack shell reads and two harness-redacted credential-shaped rows. Graded as a telemetry capture gap, not against the candidate; noting it so the capture profile for that engine's MCP and fetch calls can be checked.

gemini-baseline's prediction records input_snapshot "missing" and its reasoning reports record/context.json absent, but its transcript looked under events/<event>/record/ rather than the case-level record/, where the snapshot, context, and application text were present (the other candidate read them in the same run, and the harness-stamped context on gemini-baseline's own prediction carries snapshot_date 2026-09-01). The predictor's own data-quality flag about a missing snapshot therefore looks like a path error, not a provisioning failure; no re-provisioning is indicated.

The stored snapshot (2026-09-04) lists an amicus brief of the Initiative and Referendum Institute submitted Sep 3 2026, after the denial entry the same day; outcome.json records interim_signals.amicus_briefs = 0. Plausibly by design (counted as at disposition) — surfaced only so the outcome writer's reading is visible; no correction made and none proposed.
Missing snapshot and context.json for forward prediction on evt-order-response-requested-disposition. Proceeding using statpack baselines.

This cell's moment is response-filed, but record/documents/ carries only the application text — the September 2 response (the docket entry that opened this event) was not provisioned, so the moment's distinguishing evidence was predicted from the docket entry alone, not its content.

All three blinded predictions are marked forward but were created after the outcome's 2026-08-28 resolution date. gemini-baseline then queried the exact SCOTUS docket with all results unobserved, producing a possible-influence leakage grade; candidates a and c did not show the outcome in the staged evidence.

Decided case provisioned forward: the event resolved 2026-08-28 (application 26A256 denied by Justice Thomas), yet all three blinded candidates ran forward-mode after resolution (two on 2026-08-29, one on 2026-08-31). The committed 2026-08-31 snapshot — codex-baseline's provisioned input — itself carries the denial entry, so that cell's baseline disclosed the outcome; I graded its leakage retrieved_outcome_material=true / influenced_prediction=possible, though its prose shows no sign the entry was registered (it forecasts a September disposition). The two 2026-08-29 cells show no outcome surfacing in log or prose, but their superseded 2026-08-29 snapshot is no longer in the tree and the corpus query surface exposes case rows rather than snapshot history, so what that snapshot disclosed could not be verified. Application dockets resolve in days; a freshness check at forward provisioning would prevent this shape.

Forward cell; public pre-decision reporting (board 2-2 deadlock, signature counts, Michigan Supreme Court refusal, and the Sept 3/4 ballot deadlines) was decisive forward signal for the disposition and timing forecast — disclosed per the forward-mode hygiene note. No disposition of this application exists or was retrieved.

No record/documents/ text was provisioned for this application, and direct fetches of the supremecourt.gov application PDF and an Election Law Blog analysis both returned HTTP 403, so the application's own arguments were read only through the docket-entry title and news coverage.

The forecast materially relies on the public August 24, 2026 per curiam in Trump v. California, which predates the provisioned August 31 snapshot and was cited by both the applicants and the Solicitor General; it is legitimate forward signal and does not reveal this application's outcome.

FEC (decided June 30, 2026) and press coverage reporting FCC/DOJ support for the applicants' stay effort. The US/FCC response PDF itself was unreadable (supremecourt.gov 403s the fetcher), so the government's position is inferred from secondary coverage, not read from the filing; reasoning.md states the discount if that inference is wrong. No outcome-revealing material for 26A274 was sought or surfaced (none exists - the requested response is due Sept 3).

No disposition of 26A274 itself was surfaced. The government's response PDF on supremecourt.gov returned HTTP 403, so its position rests on the reporting, not the brief text.

The interim amicus counter undercounts on this docket: the frozen contexts and outcome.json record amicus_briefs=2 while the committed 2026-08-24 snapshot shows five amicus filings (two styled 'amicus curiae', three styled 'amici curiae' — the counter matches the singular form only). Two candidates disclosed this independently and I verified it against the snapshot. It does not affect the disposition scoring on this cell, but it conditions the harness-scored amicus-increment claim for every predictor here and will recur on any application whose amici file under the plural style.

claude-baseline's disclosed retrieval includes another predictor's committed prediction.json for the companion case scotus/9526000124 (read 'for field conventions', also yielding forward signal about the companion application). Forward-mode retrieval is unrestricted and the disclosure was honest, so this is not leakage — but it is a cross-predictor anchoring channel: predictors reading each other's committed outputs weakens the independence of the cohort's forecasts. Maintainers may want the predict prompt to speak to it.

outcome.json records interim_signals.amicus_briefs = 2, but the provisioned 2026-08-24 snapshot's docket text shows five amicus filings on Aug 3 2026 (NSL4A, 56 Former Judges, Bipartisan Former Governors, Society for the Rule of Law, Asian Law Caucus et al.). No committed prediction contents, repository history, redacted-text search, alias machinery, or alias map was read. The exposed names were disregarded, and all grading used only codex-baseline through gemini-baseline from record/blinded.

All three blinded candidate rationales report that the frozen context counted 6 amicus briefs while the August 16 snapshot contained 13 amicus docket entries; one rationale attributes the difference to singular versus plural amicus captions. The resolved outcome also records 6. Maintainers should verify whether the interim amicus counter omits plural-caption entries.

codex-baseline's staged retrieval_log.json records result_capture_coverage 1.0 but only three calls across a ten-second span (two statpack reads and one redacted credential-shaped 'other' row), while that candidate's own retrieval.md reports reading five docket-linked Supreme Court filing PDFs and making one rate-limited CourtListener MCP search. The self-reported retrieval is all pre-resolution (filings dated on or before 2026-08-12 against a 2026-08-24 resolution) so this is a capture-fidelity question, not a leakage finding — but a log that misses most of a cell's retrieval while reporting full coverage weakens the leakage grading the log exists to support.

The amicus counter undercounts this docket: the frozen contexts and the outcome's interim_signals both record amicus_briefs: 6, while the snapshot carries 13 amicus-captioned entries — the 6 captioned 'Brief amicus curiae' (singular) match the count exactly, so entries captioned 'Brief amici curiae' (plural) appear to be missed. All three candidates independently noticed this. Prediction-time and resolution-time counts are consistent with each other, so the amicus-increment claim resolves coherently, but the signal understates amicus participation by half on this case.

gaps.label: A candidate's own flags.json is not staged (by design), but where it reports a data-quality problem that the evaluator's view contradicts, there is no structured way to link the two; a flag naming the alias is the workaround.
A committed indicator of which docket-entry captions the interim amicus counter matches would have made the 6-vs-13 discrepancy checkable without re-deriving it from the snapshot text.

A conditioned interim cut by applicant class (government vs other) would let an evaluator judge the largest adjustment all three candidates made against a committed number instead of general knowledge
A per-call cutoff comparison flag in retrieval_log.json (doc date vs the prediction's frozen cutoff) would save each evaluator re-deriving it
A per-call result_capture rate varies a lot by engine (one candidate's log was entirely 'unobserved'), which limits how much a leakage grade can rest on the log rather than the candidate's own prose

A per-candidate capture-coverage summary beside the staged log (calls captured vs. calls the engine made) would make it easier to distinguish a sparse log from a genuinely quiet cell; one candidate's disclosed retrieval is largely absent from its captured log.
A stamped copy of the outcome's resolution timestamp beside each candidate's created_at would make the forward-mode sanity check one comparison instead of three file reads
A statpack cut of interim grant rate conditional on response-requested would give this moment a conditioned anchor; today the ladder columns are right-censored counts only.
A statpack cut of the interim grant rate by applicant class (government / counseled / pro se) would let the large downward adjustment made here rest on a committed number instead of cohort reasoning.
Corpus citation coverage is too sparse (159 of ~590k SCOTUS rows) for known-case prior lookup to be useful
